{'11': 'The Financial Times reports that, according to new tax disclosures, Apple paid $17 billion in corporate income tax to Ireland in 2025, accounting for 40% of its global total. Here are the details.'}

{'12': 'Apple says the figures do not reflect the full picture'}

{'13': 'According to the Financial Times, Apple paid $17 billion in taxes to Ireland last year, based on reports that new EU rules require large companies to submit.'}

{'14': "The $17 billion total includes back taxes from a long-running EU dispute. That dispute concluded in 2024, when the EU's top court ruled that Ireland had provided Apple with illegal state aid and upheld an order for the country to claw back up to €13 billion in unpaid taxes."}

{'15': 'The Financial Times adds that, according to the newly filed information, "as of September 2025, a quarter of Apple\'s global pre-tax profits were booked through its Irish entities, where only around 3% of its employees are based."'}

{'16': 'The Financial Times reports:'}

{'17': 'During its dispute with the EU, Apple consistently denied receiving illegal state aid and said it had complied with Irish tax law. Apple argued that the relevant profits originated from intellectual property developed in the United States and should therefore be taxed in the US.'}

{'18': 'However, the EU\'s top court backed the European Commission\'s position. The Commission argued that two Irish tax rulings had allowed Apple to attribute most of the profits recorded by Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe to "headquarters that had no employees or physical premises."'}

{'19': 'Returning to today\'s report, Apple told the Financial Times that it is "one of the largest taxpayers in the world" and said the newly disclosed figures do not reflect the full range of taxes it pays in different countries.'}

{'110': 'Apple noted that the figures focus on corporate income tax calculated by where assets are located, rather than other taxes (such as value-added tax) levied by where customers are based.'}
